topic_title: Top 14 Best Dog Breeds for Hot Weather
intro: Heat tolerance comes mostly from body shape and coat. Lean dogs with long legs, large ears and short single coats shed heat far better than heavy, flat-faced or thickly coated dogs. Most breeds below come from Africa, the Mediterranean or the Middle East, and many are sighthounds with strong chase instincts, so cats and small pets are a real concern. No breed is heatproof: every dog needs shade, water and walks scheduled for early morning or evening, and hot pavement can burn paws even when the air feels bearable.

picks.description: The Xoloitzcuintli, or Xolo, is the most adaptable heat-tolerant breed on this list. It comes from Mexico, and the hairless variety has no coat to trap heat; coated Xolos have a short, flat coat. It is medium in energy, calm indoors and satisfied with daily walks and some play, and the breed data rates it good with children, cats and other dogs. Grooming is minimal, but hairless dogs need skin care: sunscreen made for dogs or a light shirt in strong sun, plus occasional bathing and moisturizing to manage blackheads. The flip side of heat tolerance is cold sensitivity, so winter coats are needed in cooler months. Xolos bark little but are alert watchdogs. They usually live 12 to 14 years.
picks.best_for: Warm-climate homes with cats or kids that want a calm, easy-groom dog
picks.quirky_fact: Xolos come in three sizes, toy, miniature and standard, all considered the same breed.
picks.skip_if: You won't manage sun protection and skin care or face cold winters

picks.description: The Pharaoh Hound is a lean, medium-sized hunting hound developed in Malta, a hot Mediterranean island, and its short, fine coat and large upright ears suit warm weather. It is high in energy and needs a daily outlet for sprinting, such as a securely fenced field, plus long walks timed for cooler hours. It is friendly, playful and good with children and other dogs, but the breed data rates it not good with cats, and it will chase small animals at speed. Grooming is easy: a weekly wipe or brush keeps the coat in order and shedding is low. Pharaohs bark at a medium level and can be sensitive to harsh handling. Lifespan is about 12 to 14 years.
picks.best_for: Active owners in hot climates with a securely fenced space
picks.quirky_fact: Pharaoh Hounds are known to blush, with the nose and ears turning a deeper pink when excited.
picks.skip_if: You share the home with cats, rabbits or other small pets

picks.description: The Basenji comes from Central Africa, and its short, fine coat and compact, athletic build cope well with heat. It is medium-sized and high in energy, needing daily walks and play, and it has a strong prey drive. It is good with children and other dogs but not rated good with cats. Basenjis rarely bark, which suits close neighbors, though they make other sounds, including a yodel. Grooming is very light: they clean themselves much like cats and shed little. The trade-off is trainability, rated hard in the data. Basenjis are independent and clever, and they are known for chewing, escaping and ignoring recall. Their low cold tolerance means a jacket in winter. Lifespan is long, about 12 to 16 years.
picks.best_for: Experienced owners in warm areas who want a quiet, clean dog
picks.quirky_fact: Basenjis often yodel instead of barking, a sound sometimes called a baroo.
picks.skip_if: You have cats, need reliable off-leash recall or are a first-time owner

picks.description: The Ibizan Hound is a long-legged, medium-sized hound from the Balearic Islands of Spain, built light with large ears and a short coat that lets heat escape. It needs plenty of exercise, including chances to run hard in an enclosed area, and it is an exceptional jumper, so fences need to be tall. It is friendly and good with children and other dogs but not good with cats or small pets. The coat sheds little and needs only weekly brushing. Barking is moderate. Training is rated moderate: Ibizans learn, but their hunting instincts can override cues when they spot movement. They are generally quiet and gentle in the house once exercised. Lifespan is 12 to 14 years.
picks.best_for: Owners in warm climates with tall fencing and room to run
picks.quirky_fact: Ibizan Hounds can jump high from a standing start, a skill used for spotting prey in dense brush.
picks.skip_if: Your yard has low fencing or you keep cats or rabbits

picks.description: The Cirneco dell Etna is a small Sicilian hound bred to hunt rabbits on the slopes of Mount Etna, and its short coat and slim frame handle hot, dry weather well. It is the smallest dog on this list, which suits people who want heat tolerance without a large hound. Energy is high, so it needs daily walks plus time to run off-leash in a secure area. It is friendly, alert and good with children and other dogs, but not good with cats, and its rabbit-hunting heritage makes small pets a risk. Grooming is minimal and shedding is low. Barking is moderate, and training is rated moderate. Lifespan is about 12 to 14 years.
picks.best_for: Warm-climate owners wanting a smaller, low-grooming hunting hound
picks.quirky_fact: The Cirneco is one of the oldest Italian breeds and is still rare outside Italy.
picks.skip_if: Rabbits, guinea pigs or cats live in your home

picks.description: The Saluki is an ancient sighthound from the Middle East, bred to course game across hot desert terrain. Its lean frame and smooth coat, with light feathering on the ears and tail in some dogs, help it stay comfortable in heat. It is large and high in energy, and it needs regular chances to sprint in a secure area plus daily walks; recall is unreliable once it sights prey. Salukis are gentle, reserved and good with children and other dogs, but not with cats. Grooming is moderate: brush the feathering weekly. Barking is low, so they suit quieter homes. Training is rated moderate, and they respond best to patient, gentle methods. Lifespan is about 12 to 14 years.
picks.best_for: Calm households in hot climates with a fenced running area
picks.quirky_fact: Salukis have feathered, fur-padded feet that cushion them on rough or hot ground.
picks.skip_if: You have cats or want a dog that comes back off-leash every time

picks.description: The Sloughi is a North African sighthound from the Maghreb region, with a short, fine coat and a lean, long-legged build suited to desert heat. It is large, high in energy and athletic, needing daily exercise and safe places to gallop. Compared with some sighthounds, Sloughis are described in the data as calm, and they are loyal and somewhat reserved with strangers, preferring a quiet household. They are good with children and other dogs but not good with cats. Grooming is minimal and shedding is low, and they bark little. Training is rated moderate, and they can be sensitive to harsh handling. The breed is rare, so finding a puppy may take patience. Lifespan is about 10 to 13 years.
picks.best_for: Quiet, experienced homes wanting a calm, rare desert sighthound
picks.quirky_fact: The Sloughi is short-coated, unlike the Saluki, though the two are often confused.
picks.skip_if: You want an outgoing dog that loves visitors, or you have a cat

picks.description: The Azawakh is a tall, very lean sighthound from the Sahel region of West Africa, one of the hottest places dogs are bred, and its fine short coat and slim frame suit intense heat. It is large and high in energy, needing daily running in a secure space. It is loyal and protective, often aloof with strangers and very attached to its family. The data rates it good with children and other dogs but not with cats, and training is rated hard, so it suits experienced owners who use patient, consistent methods. Grooming is minimal and barking is low. The thin coat and low body fat mean it needs soft bedding and warmth in cold weather. Lifespan is about 10 to 13 years.
picks.best_for: Experienced sighthound owners in hot, dry climates
picks.quirky_fact: The Azawakh was traditionally kept by nomadic peoples of the Sahel as both a hunter and a camp guardian.
picks.skip_if: You have cats, are a first-time owner or want a social greeter

picks.description: The Rhodesian Ridgeback was developed in southern Africa and handles heat well thanks to its short, dense coat and athletic build. Unlike most dogs on this list, it is medium in energy, so long daily walks and some running usually satisfy an adult. It is loyal and protective, independent and intelligent, and good with children and other dogs, but not rated good with cats. Ridgebacks are large and strong, so early training matters; trainability is rated moderate and they can be stubborn. Grooming is low, with a weekly brush, and shedding is moderate. Barking is moderate. They are known for stealing food from counters. Lifespan is about 10 to 12 years.
picks.best_for: Confident owners wanting a protective, moderate-energy large dog
picks.quirky_fact: The breed's name comes from the ridge of hair along its spine that grows in the opposite direction to the rest of the coat.
picks.skip_if: You have cats or can't handle a strong, independent dog on a leash

picks.description: The Dalmatian's short, smooth coat and athletic build make it comfortable in warm weather, as long as exercise happens in cooler hours. It is medium-sized and very high in energy, originally bred to run alongside carriages, so it needs long runs or hikes daily. It is playful and good with children and other dogs, but the data rates it not good with cats. The trade-offs are significant shedding year-round, despite the short coat, and a stubborn streak, with training rated moderate. Dalmatians can be prone to deafness and urinary stones, so health-tested parents and good hydration matter, especially in heat. Barking is moderate. Lifespan is about 10 to 13 years.
picks.best_for: Runners and active families in warm climates
picks.quirky_fact: Dalmatian puppies are born white, and the spots appear over the first few weeks.
picks.skip_if: Constant shedding bothers you or you keep cats

picks.description: The Australian Cattle Dog was developed to drive cattle across hot Australian ranges, and it tolerates heat well, though its short, weather-resistant coat has an undercoat, so it ranks below the single-coated hounds. It is medium-sized and extremely high in energy, needing hard physical and mental work every day. It is loyal and protective, good with children and other dogs it knows, and not rated good with cats. Training is rated hard: Cattle Dogs learn fast but are independent and may test boundaries, and they may nip at heels. Grooming is low apart from seasonal sheds. Barking is moderate. With enough work they are devoted companions; without it they can be destructive. Lifespan is 12 to 16 years.
picks.best_for: Ranch, farm or very active owners in hot regions
picks.quirky_fact: Cattle Dog puppies are born white, and the blue or red speckled coat develops as they mature.
picks.skip_if: You want a relaxed pet, have cats or lack time for daily work

picks.description: The Anatolian Shepherd is a giant livestock guardian from the Anatolian plateau of Turkey, where summers are hot and dry, and its short, dense coat handles both heat and cold. It is medium in energy, calm and watchful rather than playful, and it needs space and a secure perimeter more than long runs. It is protective, independent and loyal, good with children and other dogs it is raised with, but not rated good with cats. Training is rated hard: Anatolians were bred to make their own decisions guarding flocks, so they are not obedience dogs. Grooming is low with heavy seasonal sheds. Barking is moderate, often at night. Lifespan is about 11 to 13 years.
picks.best_for: Rural properties needing a livestock guardian in a hot climate
picks.quirky_fact: Anatolian Shepherds have been used in Namibia to guard livestock from cheetahs.
picks.skip_if: You live in a city, have cats or want an obedient companion dog

picks.description: The Kangal Shepherd Dog is a giant Turkish livestock guardian closely related to the Anatolian, with a short, dense coat that copes with hot summers. It is medium in energy and calm when settled, but it needs land to patrol and a strong, secure fence. It is loyal and protective, good with children and other dogs in its household, and not rated good with cats. Training is rated moderate, but Kangals are independent and will act on their own judgment around strangers. Grooming is low, with seasonal shedding. Barking is moderate. Because of its size and guarding instinct, it suits experienced owners on rural property rather than suburban family life. Lifespan is about 12 to 15 years.
picks.best_for: Experienced owners with livestock or rural land in warm regions
picks.quirky_fact: The Kangal takes its name from the Kangal district of Sivas Province in Turkey.
picks.skip_if: You live in a suburb or flat, or have a cat

picks.description: The Shiba Inu is rated high for heat tolerance in our data, but it ranks last here because its thick double coat holds more heat than the coats of the hounds above, so it needs shade, cool walks and regular brushing in summer. It is small, medium in energy and clean, often grooming itself like a cat. Shibas are independent and alert; training is rated hard and recall is unreliable, so walks should stay on-leash. They are good with children and other dogs but not good with cats, and they can be possessive of food and toys. The coat sheds heavily twice a year, needing daily brushing then. Barking is moderate. Lifespan is about 12 to 15 years.
picks.best_for: Experienced owners wanting a small, clean, independent dog
picks.quirky_fact: Shibas are known for the Shiba scream, a loud shriek when they are unhappy, such as at nail trims.
picks.skip_if: You want an off-leash dog, live with cats or dislike seasonal shedding

faqs.question: What dog breed handles hot weather best?
faqs.answer: Lean, short-coated breeds from warm regions handle heat best. In this guide the Xoloitzcuintli, Pharaoh Hound and Basenji lead because they combine short or no coat with light builds. The Xolo has the extra advantage of being rated good with cats. Even these breeds need shade, water and walks in the cooler parts of the day during heat waves.

faqs.question: Should I shave my dog's coat in summer?
faqs.answer: Not for double-coated breeds such as the Shiba Inu. The undercoat and guard hairs help insulate against heat and protect the skin from sunburn, and shaved double coats can grow back unevenly. Regular brushing to remove loose undercoat helps air move through the coat. Short single-coated dogs need no trimming, but pale and hairless dogs need sun protection instead.

faqs.question: What temperature is too hot to walk a dog?
faqs.answer: There is no single safe number, because humidity, sun, pavement and the dog's build all matter. A simple check is to hold the back of your hand on the pavement for several seconds; if it is uncomfortable for you, it is too hot for paws. In hot weather, walk early or late, choose shaded grass and bring water.

faqs.question: Are hot-weather breeds good with cats?
faqs.answer: Most are not. Of the breeds in this guide, only the Xoloitzcuintli is rated good with cats in our breed data. Many of the others are sighthounds or hunting breeds bred to chase small, fast animals, and training does not reliably remove that instinct. If you already have a cat, choose the Xolo or look beyond this list.

faqs.question: What are the signs of heatstroke in a dog?
faqs.answer: Warning signs include heavy, fast panting, thick drool, bright red or pale gums, weakness, stumbling, vomiting or collapse. Move the dog to shade or air conditioning, offer small amounts of cool water, wet the body with cool rather than ice-cold water, and contact a vet right away. Heatstroke can be fatal even when the dog seems to recover.

seo_title: Best Dog Breeds for Hot Weather (2026 Guide)
answer: The Xoloitzcuintli, Pharaoh Hound and Basenji are the best hot-weather dogs here: lean, short-coated breeds from warm regions. Coat type is the deciding factor, so favor short single coats over dense double coats, and still walk any dog in the cooler hours.
method: We filtered a 150-breed dataset for breeds rated highly tolerant of heat, then ordered them by coat and build, putting hairless and short single-coated breeds first and dense or double-coated breeds last, with household fit used to break ties.
author: Elena Marsh
